info.title: Critical Review: Decoupling the RDL Chain — Findings and Negative Inventory

abstract.para: A critical evaluation of the skills exercised during the decoupling, the verified findings surfaced (each self-referential — defects in the very chain doing the work), and the mandatory negative inventory required by the RDL honesty mandate.

section.title: Critical evaluation of the skills used
section.para: The RDL orchestrator held discipline well: the phase structure forced research before design and tests before implementation, and the truth-type gate caught claims that were only training-recall (the industry-standard citations) and routed them through web verification before they were written into skills. Its weakness is the subject of Finding 1: its anti-silent-failure machinery had a loophole its author did not see.

The research-phase scope/truth-type discipline was the highest-value component; without it the standards would have been asserted from memory. The rdl-brainstorming and rdl-writing-plans sub-skills were the easiest to decouple because their idiosyncrasy was only a reference to the plugin's process; the process itself is a generic, well-documented discipline that inlined cleanly. The scholarly-white-paper skill is the subject of Findings 2 and 3.

section.title: Finding 1 — The chain permitted discretionary deferral of in-scope work
section.para: In the first scholarly summary, three in-scope items were deferred on the author's own judgement of proportionality (disproportionate, a follow-up), using the logged skip mechanism and the negative inventory's deferred category as exits. The user identified this as evidence of a defect.

Root-cause analysis: the chain elsewhere states a Rice-correct principle — triviality and effort are undecidable and must not be auto-judged; scope may be reduced only by explicit user assertion — but that principle lived only in the brainstorming sub-skill's notation valve and was never propagated to the orchestrator's phase discipline. The skip/prompt rule authorised skips only for missing capability grants, yet nothing prevented an agent from relabelling an effort judgement as a logged skip. This is confirmed: it reproduced in a single session with the very agent that authored the anti-silent-failure rules.

Repair: the orchestrator now states that the only valid basis for skipping is a missing capability grant; proportionality is never a skip reason; scope-out requires an explicit user-asserted exception; and a deferral resting on agent discretion is a false-clean. Guarded by test_no_discretionary_deferral.py.

section.title: Finding 2 — Phase 5's toolchain requirement was never declared
section.para: The RDL claims that each skill's requirements are elevated to a declared, resolved-up-front manifest. Yet Phase 5 invokes scholarly-white-paper, whose canonical format needs a DocBook, RELAX NG, and XSLT toolchain (xmllint, xsltproc, jing), and neither the orchestrator nor the project manifest ever named or granted those tools. The requirement was invisible until the phase was actually reached, at which point the author improvised rather than following a pre-declared requirement — precisely the failure the manifest model exists to prevent.

Repair: the orchestrator's Phase 5 now declares the toolchain and ties it to the skip/prompt rule (missing tool names the exact install and prompts); the project manifest grants the toolchain in [capabilities].subprocess. Guarded by test_phase5_toolchain_declared.py. The tools were then installed and the paper rendered, closing the loop the manifest model predicts.

section.title: Finding 3 — The scholarly-white-paper skill's own example does not validate
section.para: The skill instructs authors to place a title as a sibling immediately after an XIncluded info block, and to carry Dublin Core as foreign-namespace dc:* elements inside info. Against the DocBook 5.0 RELAX NG schema packaged in Debian bookworm (docbook5-xml), this fails: the article content model rejects the sibling title. The caveat is that the skill targets DocBook 5.2, whose RNG is not distro-packaged; the failure is confirmed against the 5.0 baseline actually available, and a 5.2 environment might differ. The paper was authored in the validating pattern instead (title inside info; Dublin Core in a bibliomisc carrier), and validates under both xmllint --relaxng and jing.

section.title: Finding 4 — Decoupled prose, re-coupled diagram (found by a recursive loop)
section.para: A subsequent RDL loop whose subject was the RDL skill itself found that the decoupling had been applied to the prose and the standards table but not to the state-machine diagram: its nodes still named the superpowers skills as the phase method (verification-before-completion, finishing-a-development-branch, systematic-debugging) and the skill-gap edge still pointed to writing-skills / skill-creator. The diagram directly contradicted the same document's claim that the loop never requires the plugin.

Crucially, the 83-test suite did not catch this. The existing guardrail (test_no_hard_superpowers_invocation) matched only the imperative pattern invoke/inherit superpowers:; the bare skill base-names in the diagram carried no superpowers: prefix and passed every test. This is a concrete instance of the paper's own negative-inventory item 1 — a grep-clean, test-green result is not a decoupled result — reproduced against the decoupling work itself one turn later. Repair: the diagram now names each phase's standard (Root-Cause Analysis, Definition of Done and V&V, GitHub Flow, the Agent Skills format), and a credit-block-aware guardrail (test_state_machine_decoupled.py) bans any reference-implementation skill name outside the explicit credit block while asserting the diagram positively names each standard.

section.title: Mandatory negative inventory
section.para: The honesty mandate requires that every scholarly paper answer four questions about what the positive claims do not cover.

listitem.para: Claimed but not demonstrated by any test. That the loop behaviourally runs to completion with Superpowers physically uninstalled. The guardrails prove the source text contains no invocations (a static, regex proxy); no test executes the full loop in a plugin-absent runtime. Equally, that each cited standard is applied faithfully — the citations were verified as real standards, but no test asserts the mapping is not a plausible-but-wrong analogy.

Silent-failure modes the tests cannot see. The frontmatter linter parses flat single-line YAML; a multi-line block-scalar description would be mis-parsed silently rather than rejected. The DocBook source validates against DocBook 5.0, not the 5.2 the skill names; content that is valid 5.0 but malformed 5.2 would pass here and fail elsewhere without warning.

Failure before any hook fires. The no-invocation guardrail is a regex; a future skill that legitimately needs to invoke a plugin skill would be rejected as re-coupling, a false positive with no encoded escape hatch. And the Rice-correct rule depends on the agent honestly surfacing scope decisions to the user for assertion; an agent that simply does not raise the question defeats it, and no hook can detect a question that was never asked.

Explicitly deferred, with a legitimate basis. Nothing is deferred on author discretion in this pass. The DocBook-to-PDF step (pdflatex) is produced only if the LaTeX output is well-formed; PDF is an optional output per the skill and is a grant-based, named skip if it fails, not a silent one. No user-asserted exception was taken.

section.title: Limitations
section.para: The decoupling is verified structurally and by a green 83-test suite, but the strongest claim — plugin-absent behavioural completion — remains a static proxy rather than a live demonstration. The standards were verified as existing and current; their faithful application is argued, not machine-checked. The historical design documents retain plugin references by design, as dated records, now marked superseded.
